utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon. There are two matters I would like to deal with before we proceed with the evidence. A motion has been made to us to modify the Scheduling Order of the 15th of November, 2006, made on behalf of all accused and heartily endorsed by the Prosecution. The Judges all hope that in years to come you'll look back on the submissions in both the motion and the Prosecution response and smile to yourselves. We hope that you all counsel have long and healthy lives ahead of you, and we assure you that we have taken account of your submissions yet again on this issue. But we take the opportunity to remind you also of the periods available for intensive preparation, both over the December and January break, at Easter, as we've indicated, and also much later in the year. We are also happy to give you an indication that we will be open to persuasion from time to time that there should be a long weekend, perhaps even once a month, particularly in months where there is not another break in the proceedings. So, for example, February, March are months where we consider that may be an appropriate course, depending on the progress we are making. But we re-emphasise our reason for seeking to make further progress at this stage is the availability of courtroom space, the need to ensure a fair and expeditious trial, and the sure and certain knowledge that at some stage later in this trial there will be interruptions and we have to have spare capacity in the tank to deal with these. We have previously also made it clear to you that we accept that, for example, when you get towards the end of the Prosecution case there will inevitably be hiccups that we have to accommodate to ensure that the case is tied together adequately. But in exchange for recognising that, we hope that you will appreciate the need for added effort when there is time available to build up that reserve that will be in everybody's long-term interests. So we have decided to refuse the motion. The other matter that I can deal with now, I think, is protective measures for Witness K56. This -- the Chamber is entirely satisfied that there have to be additional trial-related protective measures and entirely satisfied that these must include a means of concealing the identity of the witness. Voice and image distortion would appear, on the face of it, to be adequate except for certain parts of the evidence. And it may be that there are certain parts where it is felt that the content of the evidence itself would sufficiently identify the witness and thus put him at risk. So unless, Mr. Hannis, you have anything more to submit on this, what we would propose is putting in place voice and image distortion and inviting you to apply for private session as necessary in the course of the evidence. Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes we understand that -- and it may be a matter that we have to judge as we go along to see whether or not it works that way. It's the kind of witness who we may have to go in and out often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I know sometimes that's cumbersome. But I take your point, we want to be in public as much as we can, as often as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other option, but we don't favour this, is to have it in closed session, then review it and decide whether the bulk of it can be made public. But the practice of the Tribunal appears to be to involve -- appears to involve consulting a witness about the change in the status of his evidence at a later stage, and that's something we would like to avoid having to do. We would rather put in place adequate measures from the outset of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will try and -- we will try and deal with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we had also requested a new pseudonym for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that will also be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I say one thing in regard to your first decision on that motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: November is a month where we don't otherwise have a break and would you consider the possibility of a day off this month?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I recognise that you'll have the support of at least six parties for that, but it's just a pity it comes that bit too late, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I say that half in jest, Your Honour, but half seriously as well in anticipation of our available witnesses in the coming week and the fact that we had -- in part it's a knock-on effect from Mr. Tanic, whose cross-examination was so long, and understandably so. But General DZ was intended to be the first witness this week for two days, but because he had to be somewhere else Wednesday we had to send him back and he cannot return until the 4th of December, which, all other things considered, we are going to have some problems next week, I think, unless one other matter, a witness we had subpoenaed back in October, Mr. Sladjan Markovic we will be submitting to your Court -- to Your Honours a report on our efforts to try and get him served with a subpoena and here. And that's been another hole in our schedule because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I note what you say, Mr. Hannis, but this is also a very serious point. If you actually sit down and look at the time that we have allocated for the presentation of the Prosecution case and try to work out when it is likely to end, you will be surprised, I suspect -- perhaps you've already done it, but if you haven't done it, I invite you to do so because you may well be surprised by how long it will take. There are still indeterminate elements in the time allocated. There's also, of course, the question, if you do make speedier-than-anticipated progress, whether you may be able to introduce more evidence in support of aspects that you feel have perhaps not come up to expectation. So there are many good reasons, I think, for getting our heads down at the moment and keeping going, knowing that we can later accommodate particular requirements that arise. Now, Ms. Kravetz, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The next Prosecution witness is Dr. Helge Brunborg. Dr. Brunborg is our demographic expert. His evidence is primarily relevant to paragraphs 19 and 81 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record and spell your last name.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My full name is Helge Brunborg. My last name Brunborg is spelled B-r-u-n-b-o-r-g.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we are going to be speaking the same language today, I'm going to ask you to pause after every question to allow the interpreters sufficient time to do the translation. Mr. Brunborg, you are of Norwegian nationality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I am a demographer, a researcher in demography.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe your educational background for the Court.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I have studied mathematics, statistics and economics at the university of Oslo with something similar to masters degree, and I have a PhD in economics from University of Michigan specialising in demography.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where you employed, Mr. Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm employed by Statistics Norway in Oslo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What is Statistics Norway?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is the government institution for statistics of Norway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Your CV --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Which is, Your Honours, Exhibit P2503.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- sets out in full detail your academic and profession backgrounds and activities and your publications. We are not going to go through all of that today. I would just like to focus on some aspects of your professional background. Could you tell us about your experience in the field of demography applied to conflict situations?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I started to work here in June 1997 on a sort of trial basis because the Tribunal felt there was a need for somebody who is professionally in the area of demography and population statistics, and I looked at the -- especially at the demographic consequences of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1992 and 1995. So I worked until the end of 1998 as a consultant. Since then, one or two years after I left, a permanent position was established for that kind of job and a permanent office to do demographic work and population statistics. And I have also since then become interested in this field from scientific point of view and initiated a Working Group under the International Union for the Scientific Study of Population. The Working Group was called the Demography of Conflict and Violence. It has later been continued and changed its name into the demography of armed conflicts, and we have arranged seminars and published journals and a book soon coming out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you previously testified as an expert witness in this Tribunal in other cases?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In which cases did you testify?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Krstic, Blagojevic, and Milosevic, although the last testimony was interrupted because of poor health. So there was no -- it was not continued nor completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand. Other than your participation as an expert witness in these cases and your preparation of the report that deals with Kosovo which is the subject of your testimony here today, have you been otherwise engaged in work in the Balkans in your field of demography?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I am involved in a project in Albania to advise on modernising the civil status system, the system for registering population and events. So my -- I'm advising on that project from a distance from Oslo. I never lived in Albania. I go there once or twice a year for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I know you prepared your CV some time ago. Do you want to provide any additional updates to your CV, either regarding current activities that you're carrying out in your work in Oslo or recent publications that you have been involved in?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I guess the only thing I should mention is that I'm now in charge of a very large survey in Norway called generations and gender programme, as part of an international programme, where people from age 18 to 79 are interviewed about aspects of life, work, births, employment, et cetera. And I've also published then the journals that I mentioned and a book is coming out soon on conflict demography.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender Dr. Brunborg's CV at this time. This is Exhibit P2503.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Brunborg, in 2002 you were asked by the Office of the Prosecution to prepare a report on the size and composition, ethnic composition, of Kosovo prior to the conflict, the 1999 conflict. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain how you went about to gather your data to prepare this report.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I was provided first with -- by the OTP by a report by UNFPA and some French demographers on the survey conducted in Kosovo in 1999 and 2000. Secondly, I searched internet. Thirdly, I went to the library of Statistics Norway, which happens to have a very good collection of statistics on the former Yugoslavia. So that's where I -- actually, in the basement of Statistics Norway was where I found most of the information I needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before submitting this report to the Office of the Prosecution, was it subjected to peer review?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not strictly speaking, but I had several colleagues read it and comment upon it. Actually, three Norwegian colleagues, one Dutch, and one Serbian colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did the Office of the Prosecution have any input as to the conclusions of your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not at all. But they did read and provided some sort of editorial advice, since English is not my first language.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, could you briefly summarise the conclusions of your report on the size and ethnic composition of Kosovo for the Court.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, the problem, as I see it, is that there are no good data for Kosovo, especially for the Albanian population. The Albanian population boycotted the 1991 census. There was no census since then. There was one in 2001, but that is after the period -- I was asked to look only at the population development until 1998. And so there are data on births and deaths but not on migration, which is a very important factor to determine the population size and composition. So the most important source of information then was the -- what I will call the French UN survey, a sample survey, which asked people in households in Kosovo whether somebody had moved away from the household in their last years and whether they had come back. So that gave an estimate of the absent population or absent household members. In addition, since in my -- also there were complete households that left. An estimate was made of the difference in population size if there had been no out migration from Kosovo. By comparing the 1981 population size and the Blayo -- that is the French demographer, he was the first author of that report, I will refer to it as the Blayo report, if that is all right. They also gave an estimate of the population in 1999 and 1998. So the difference between a hypothetical population without any out migration and the recorded population in 1998, could then be ascribed to out migration. And since they had asked about when people left, they got a distribution of out migration for each year from 1981 to 1998, and in that way they got the population size.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the French demographers had conducted a sample survey. How were they -- if you're aware, how were they able to determine whether the sample that they had taken was representative of the estimated population of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it was an area sample survey and they drew randomly -- they sampled some -- I think it was 34 rural areas and a number of urban areas. Within each of these, they sampled some small -- a smaller area and interviewed everybody in those areas, every person, every household. They also -- but a sample survey cannot give total population size, of course. But then they compared that to a UNHCR survey, that is the High Commissioner for Refugees, survey where they had asked village administrators, that was in November 1999, I believe, about the population size in each. And they found that, on average, the French sample survey constituted 2 and a half per cent of the total population. And in that way, they could get estimates of the total population in 1999, the fall of 1999, 1st of November, in fact, and then they could backtrack, project backwards the population as of the 1st of October, 1998, which was before the conflict, and that was what I was asked to look at, the population until 1998, considering then population growth in the period and those who might -- out migrated from Kosovo in late 1998 and the first half of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you aware of how this French survey was funded. Who sponsored and who funded this survey?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was funded by UNFPA, that is the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, and IOM, International Organisation for Migration, and operationally I also received some assistance from the Kosovo Institute of Statistics -- and the French demographers served as advisors in designing questionnaire, data entry, and analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who conducted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just ask you. Can I ask you two questions about this. I hadn't understood part of your previous answer where you said that they compared that to a UNHCR survey in November 1999 about the population size in each and they found that on average the French sample survey constituted 2 and a half per cent of the total population. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you draw a sample -- if I go out and every -- interview every people in every fifth house in The Hague, I will get a sample of persons, a sample population, but I don't -- I would need to know the total population to know the percentage of -- that has been sampled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, in other words, they sampled 2 and a half per cent of the total population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And then they used that to estimate the total population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. The second question I have is related to it. In your report on the second page when you're dealing with the UNHCR estimate, you say: "They also made a de jure estimate for 1998 as an extrapolation of the 1991 census population." Now, if the census was boycotted, how did they do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the federal -- the Institute of Statistics for the former Yugoslavia made a projection from 1981 to 1991 because the Albanians boycotted the population, taking into account the best estimates they had on fertility and mortality rates and that was -- then became the official estimate of the population of Kosovo for 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's the figure that was then used by UNHCR as a starting point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you had just explained that the French demographers helped to design this survey. Did they collaborate with someone in Kosovo who actually conducted this survey on the ground?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't know the details, but it says in the acknowledgements and that they cooperated with the statistical office of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, based on your experience, how reliable are the estimates regarding the size of the population given in this French report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, there are of course several degrees of uncertainty, but I think in general it is quite reliable. But it's unreliable enough that the demographers have -- they've given a range of the figure. They cannot know exactly. They -- it says -- excuse me. I have to look it up. Between 2.044 and 2.131 persons in Kosovo as of the 1st October 1998. So there is a range due to, for example, the sampling variation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- apart from consulting this specific survey, did you also look at other sources, specifically sources from the former Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I looked at all the sources that I could find from the federal institute of statistics, also called the federal statistical office, previously the socialist federal statistical office, and their estimates are very consistent with these other estimates from -- for the 1990s, and there's not much difference. There is a time trend and a more or less continuous line from 1948 until 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know what was the source data used by the federal statistic office to draw up those numbers that you referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah, basically two sources. One is the census, population censuses, that were conducted in almost every year, 1948, 1951, 1961, 1971, 1981, and 1991, with some deficiency. And in addition, they have the vital statistics, that is the number of births and deaths in each year, which is recorded by the local offices and transferred to the main office in Kosovo and Belgrade. That is the natural population growth. So if you have -- in a year you have the population size given by the census, and then you have the natural growth, that is the difference between births and deaths, you can then accumulate and get, five years later, population size, but except for migration. So then -- then either you have to give an estimate of the migration or, if that is not available, say, well, this is what we call the de jure population. Those who left are included because many of them may be coming back. Maybe they are only temporarily abroad for work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred to the de jure population. What is the difference between de jure and de facto population?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: De facto population is the number of people who are actually in the country. De jure is those who are usually in the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So I understand from your answer that the number -- estimates of the federal statistics office are -- refer only to the de jure population?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Mostly, but not only, because they have also given some de facto population estimates, are found in the tables. And I'm not quite sure how they were arrived at, but they are generally 20 to 90.000 lower than the de jure estimates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there other sources from the region that you consulted when preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I searched internet also for unofficial sources and I found something from federal institute -- no, federal secretariat of information and some articles by individual authors and checked the numbers and found generally, I'm sorry to say, that they were not very reliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Why are you saying that they were not reliable, these estimates?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Methodology was poor. There was no reference to sources, no scientific basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How did these estimates compare to the other ones that you had consulted from the federal statistic office?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The ones by the federal secretariat of information, 1998, and also by Grecic 1999 gave a number that was much, much lower for the population size than the other numbers. In fact, only 1.4 million for 1998 versus, excuse me, 2.2 or 2.1 by the federal statistical office. And it's not conceivable that the population could have developed in that -- dropped so fast in only one year or so. Their reasoning was based on a comparison apparently between the population development in developing countries -- in other countries, that is Macedonia and Albania, saying, that, well, these Albanians developed in the same way, but there's no -- there's no basis for making that assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just -- may I ask you one other question about the federal statistical office figures. You have your report in front of you, your original report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at the first page of that, in the bottom paragraph you have certain estimates from that office. If you go to the next page, in the second paragraph you talk there of the de facto estimates for 1997 and 1998, and the first one you quote is the federal statistics office figure. On the earlier paragraph, that figure of 2.188.000 appears as a de jure figure for 1997, and the de facto figure appears to be 2.166 -- should the second paragraph on page 2 actually be 2.166.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be -- you're absolutely correct. That is a misprint. I'm sorry. On the table on page 13, the de facto figure for 1997 is given by the FSO as 2.116 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, maybe that is a -- 166, I did not see -- oh, yeah, I need to check that, whether it is 2.166 or 2.116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the other connected question I wish to ask you relates to the year that this estimate was prepared. Is there a footnote identifying the particular document from which these figures come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have a footnote 8, is that the one or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They're all given on page 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 13, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the right-hand column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's the 1998 version and, is that right, the source is a 1998 document and it looks as though the figure should be 2.116?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg, you have referred in your evidence to the issue of migration and the impact of migration in calculating your estimates. Could you just briefly explain how you dealt with the issue of out migration from Kosovo when calculating the conclusions of your report, the numbers that you give.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I looked at the figures given by the Blayo, the French demographer, and their distribution of migration by year, and actually it was Chantal Blayo and her colleagues that used that to make an estimate of the population size in 1998. They subtracted then an estimate of the population in 1998/1999. So they distributed the migration -- actually, over all the years, 1981 and forward, to give -- to be consistent with the population figure in -- in theirs in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And their source for this data was, again, the UNHCR --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was their own survey but compared with the UNHCR headcount.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have the report up in e-court; it's P160. And could we go to page 14 in the English and 15 in the B/C/S -- 196, I'm sorry, I misspoke. 1960. Just to correct the transcript, it's P1960. Could we zoom in on figure 2, yes, scroll down. There.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg, we have here a figure of the total population of Kosovo. Could you comment on what is illustrated here in this graph.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, first it shows a very rapid population growth since 1948; and secondly, it gives both de jure and some de facto figures; and thirdly, it gives several estimates for the last years. There is Islami for 1995, and there's the UNHCR and Blayo and federal secretariat of information for 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now go to figure 4, which is on page 16 of the English and 17 of the B/C/S version of the report. And could we -- yes, there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This figure, Dr. Brunborg, relates to the ethnic composition of the population. Could you briefly comment on what is illustrated here.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it shows that the -- generally since 1950, the Albanian proportion of the population has increased from between 60 and 70 per cent to around 80 per cent in 1991 and that there is considerably variation for 1995 and 1998. But as I said, the federal secretariat of information estimate is much -- is most likely to low and the Islami estimate is most likely too high. So the UNHCR estimate is, most likely I would say, the best one and it gives a slightly higher than 80 per cent Albanians, and vice versa for the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. So the source that you relied on for your conclusions on the ethnic composition of Kosovo, would that be the UNHCR report which is illustrated here?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to the addendum that you prepared with regard to this report, could you give us the reasons for this addendum, why you had to prepare it.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor asked me to write an addendum because they had received new information from Belgrade on their request, I believe, and so they asked me to look at it and write an addendum report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was this new information that you looked at to prepare your addendum?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: There was a letter from the federal Ministry of Justice, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and a report from the federal statistics bureau of 2002 and a book with census results from 1993. So I looked at all of this. The census results book I had seen before, so that didn't add anything. I read the report. There was no new data of interest here. There were -- because there was still no data on migration. I was anxious to see hard data on migration and I wish there were. But there wasn't any, so the conclusions were the same. That report said more about population growth in Kosovo and the other republics in the former Yugoslavia and compared and highlighted the extraordinary nature of the Kosovo population, where fertility remained high much longer than the other republics, high number of children per woman, and the decline did not start there until the early 1990s, unlike the other republics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did these new sources that you consulted, did they have any impact on the previous conclusions that you had given in your original report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not really. They underlined the uncertainty of the numbers for Kosovo because of the boycott of the Albanian population in 1991, and all censuses since then, and the lack of migration data. And it highlighted the high population growth due to very high fertility in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to tender Dr. Brunborg's report at this stage. This is P1960, and the addendum to this report P1961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order will be: General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, General Lukic, Mr. Sainovic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brunborg, good afternoon. My name is Tomislav Visnjic, Defence counsel for General Ojdanic. I'm going to ask you a few questions linked to your work, your report, and I'm going to ask you for some clarifications, which I would like to have with respect to how you arrived at your conclusions and the data and information that you used to compile the report. From your introduction as well as from your biography, your CV, I understood it that you are first and foremost an economist, judging by your education, and then later on during your work you decided to focus on demography. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, actually, I think I would say I became a demographer during my final studies of economics in Oslo, and I went to the United States to pursue my interest in demography. But there was no demography programme as such at the University of Michigan, so I had to take a PhD in economics but specialising in demography. So I consider myself a demographer today and a rather poor economist, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you shortly explain to us what data a demographer needs, which -- what data is indispensable for them to be able to evaluate the exact percentage of populations in Kosovo in 1990 or at any other year when there is no population census -- register and the last population census was taken more than 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, then there is -- there are two ways of going about it. One is to project the population from the last known -- the last date when the population was known with accuracy. Projected by age and sex, taking fertility rates into consideration, that is the number of births per woman, and mortality, how many die who in each age, and, if available, migration data. That is one way of going about it. The second is to do a survey. Ideally there should have been a census, but for many reasons that was not done. A census is a very complicated and large undertaking and cannot be done on short notice. So this sample survey that was conducted -- funded by UNFPA and conducted by French demographer was an attempt to get an estimate of the population. Actually, in 1999 after the war, but then the data were collected in such a way that it could also be used to estimate the population size before the conflict started.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly then there are three elements. One would be the basic year from when you start your estimations; the second would be data about births and deaths; and the third element would be information and data about migration. Would those be the three basic elements?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: But if I may add, migration -- there's always two streams, there's out migration and in migration, sometimes combined into net migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, I said migration, but of course it would be more precise to use both those in and out terms. Now, since we're on the subject of population census, for high-quality estimations of population to be carried out, the basic year should be the year in which the population census was taken. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And as you yourself said in your report on page 4, chapter 3, of your 2002 report, you said: "The most usual method for estimating the number and composition of the population is to carry out a population census and a census of the households." And I would add to that that that would be the best method. Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak closer to the microphones, please, for the interpreter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand from what you said, the last population census in Kosovo-Metohija was conducted in 1981. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, there was one in 1991, but as I said, it was boycotted by the Albanian population but not by other population groups. So there is a -- there are partial estimates for 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So as far as 1991 is concerned, we, in fact, do not have a population census; all we have is an estimate of the population. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: There are estimates of the total population, but there are counts of non-Albanian population groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you there. So that means that in the total number, if we were to give the total number of the population, it is nonetheless a percentage, because it is in two parts, the estimate part and the actual count part. So the number is added to give us the population sample and the estimate. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know of any case - I assume that we're dealing with the 20th century - in which the population totally boycotted a population census, either one part of the population boycotted it or some other part boycotted it? If you take a look at Europe, can you quote any example of that kind, because I see that according to your curriculum vitae you carried out investigations of this kind in various countries.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, the only case I can think of is Germany where there hasn't been a population census for many years because for political resentment of enumeration. So they are estimating the population in other ways. There are more and more countries in Europe that do not conduct censuses because -- either because there is some political resentment or because they can get the information from other sources, like my own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When we say that, and if you mean Germany, do we mean the 1990s in Germany when there were problems over the questionnaire? Is that what you mean? Am I right there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think it was earlier, but I'm not quite sure. I think it was earlier. I think the last census in Germany was in the 1975, was it? I'm not quite sure about that, I'm afraid. And the reason is the resentment against this -- what we could call big brother; that is, the government wants to know too much about its population. And that's why many people -- if many people are against it, that weakens the quality of the census, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you happen to know who, according to the population census, according to the law in 1981 on the population census, had the exclusive right to exert supervision and control over a population census in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Who? It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Which organ, which body.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I believe it was first the institute in office in Belgrade and -- which delegated responsibility to each republic and autonomous province. The census was carried out on the same day, same period, in all six republics and two autonomous provinces, and basically the same questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would you perhaps agree with me if I tell you that the population census in Kosovo and Metohija in 1981 and 1991 was under the exclusive authority of Kosovo statistics, or rather, the provincial institute for statistics of Kosovo, whereas the methodology, that is to say the forms and questionnaires used, were prescribed by the federal institute. So the census itself, the investigators, researchers, and other data were done in the Kosovo institute for statistics. Do you happen to know that as a fact?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't know the details, but I think your description is more or less right. The questionnaire was designed in Belgrade, and the survey was conducted in each republic. I'm mostly familiar with Bosnia in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And would you -- I see that in your answer here you say "in all the republics." I might add all the republics and provinces, in view of the fact that as far as Kosovo is concerned. I know that you don't perhaps understand the difference in terms, but as far as Kosovo is concerned, the gathering of data, control, and supervision of the material and the results were fully processed by the local institute for statistics, which was led by the local authorities, of course.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, I'm fully aware that the two autonomous provinces, Vojvodina and Kosovo and Metohija, had their own statistical offices and was given responsibility for conducting the actual census operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you will agree with me when I say that in the absence of official statistical data, the possibility for manipulation with the number of inhabitants is fairly great. When I say "manipulation," I mean political manipulation.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct. If there are no data --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there are no data, data can be manipulated, of course, but there are ways of checking demographic data, whether they are consistent and reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said -- or, rather, you told the Court that you gathered certain information and data from the UNHCR, if I remember, and also from -- and also those relating to the period after 1999. Now, my question is this: Do you know that the Assembly of Kosovo enacted a law on population census in August 2003, already then, but that nothing has been done since about that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what's the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the relevance of that question is in the following. There are methods in existence in demography - and I think the expert can help us out here - on the basis of which -- on the basis of later data you can compare earlier data and then find a mean, an average. So there was nothing against -- it's nothing against the Assembly of Kosovo and nothing topical. It was just a technical attempt to calculate a piece of information, a piece of data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what? Even if it's right. This evidence is about what the actual position was in 1998, not about whether it ought to have been sorted out since. I'm not following the relevance of the fact that there is a way of working things out later. Let's concentrate on what matters here. Even the very question of who conducted the -- or who were responsible administratively for the conduct doesn't appear to me to be relevant. Let's focus the cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'll put the question this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, is it true that not even after 1999 to the present day there are authentic data of the Kosovo statistical system about the number, the precise number, of inhabitants in Kosovo, although that system is being helped out by various experts nowadays?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I have not followed this in detail, so I'm not aware -- I'm not aware of any census in Kosovo after -- or any other new data, that is correct, but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your report you conclude that the population of Kosovo in the period prior to the 1998/1999 conflict was between 2 and 2.2 million inhabitants, and that is the 12th of September, 2003, report. Am I right in saying that? Paragraph 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And from your report of the 14th of August, 2002, you conclude that in 1998 in Kosovo there were 1.7 million Albanians, about 200.000 Serbs, and about 140.000 members of other ethnic groups. Am I right? And that's on page 2 of your report.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, did you perhaps consult the UNMIK report on population for the year 2000 on the basis of the lists for the elections?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was not aware and I did not look for sources that far into the future because I was only asked to look at the population in 1998 -- before 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. However, you also did expertise in 2002 and 2003. Now, had you known about those data from the electoral lists, would you have used them? Would you have taken them into consideration?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I worked with electoral lists for other countries, and they give you on an individual basis name and date of birth, et cetera, of all the voters eligible. I don't really see how I could have used those lists to reconstruct the population of Kosovo in 1998 if there was nothing on when -- about whether these voters had left the country or not, or returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But a moment ago we weren't discussing the fact that what you did have as a basis, as your groundwork for 1998 and 1999, was also an estimation. So what you're telling me now, whether certain voters went out to vote, left the country, returned or not, that's also an estimation, but at least we have a fixed list as opposed to the data we didn't have previously; that is to say, the 2000 list.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe that a voters' list does not usually contain information about immigration or emigration, so I don't see how it could have been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you that for two reasons, first because in your previous work you used the electoral lists, the voting lists, and the other expertise that you did before this court; and secondly, because it seems to me that the voting lists are more reliable from the different estimations, especially as you in your report on page 1 of your 2003 report said yourself that you had the chance of seeing new material which emphasised the great unreliability of the population data for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Now, there's one strong weakness of voters' lists. One is that it only includes people who registered to vote; and secondly, it does not include people under the age of 18 usually. So it would give a very partial view of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I agree with you on that point, but at least for this category it is fairly precise. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It is not precise for 1998. It may be precise for 2002 or whatever, but not for a previous year. It's a snap-shot in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the basis of the data from the 2000 elections, UNMIK assessed that in the year 2000 the number of inhabitants of Kosovo was 2.105.000, and that according to a survey the demographic, social, and reproductive situation in Kosovo conducted by the United Nations, that is the UNPHA, which was probably the United Nations population fund, the number of inhabitants assessed for 2000 was roughly 1.9 to 2.2 million, of which 88 per cent are Albanians, 7 per cent are Serbs, and 5 per cent others. Do you know about those facts and figures?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One interesting feature from these, Mr. Brunborg, is the 1.9 to 2.2 million is fairly consistent with our own figure. However, the estimate of Serb and other percentage of the population is, on the face of it, significantly lower. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this, of course, is after traumatic events in 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly that is what I would have liked to add myself. We know about the first, the large migration streams of Albanians in 1999, and later of Serbs from Kosovo. So that the figures are somewhat different in 2002 is no surprise at all. In fact, as you observed, Your Honour, I thought that the figures were remarkably consistent with the previous estimates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we going somewhere particular with this, Mr. Visnjic, that's going to illuminate the question of the population prior to 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not my intention to show that the ratio of the population before and after -- to show it before 1999 and after 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But I wanted to ask the witness what you asked him as well, whether he would agree with me that this estimate for the year 2000, if it is problematic, whether he would agree with me that it was compiled by experts, UNMIK experts on the spot, working on location, who had direct sources, as opposed to the sources that you used which were, to a certain extent, indirect. Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I have no information about the collection of the voters' list data, but generally the voters' list are compiled in a completely different way, usually by voters coming to centres to register. And there are many people who don't come, and the methodology is so different that it's difficult to compare, usually, the estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly: Are you saying to us here that in fact this UNMIK estimate on the basis of the voters' lists is less relevant, in view of the difficulties you have presented?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It is less relevant, but it's still surprisingly close to the other estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now -- in fact, Mr. Brunborg, let me ask you directly: Did you, in fact, in gathering this data use direct data from Kosovo statistics or, rather, the present institute for statistics of Kosovo or the previous provincial institute for statistics of Kosovo? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I used only data that were published by the institute in Belgrade for all of the country, and they have received, I believe, some of the data from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And do you know that from 1997, data from Kosovo were not relayed back to the institute, but that the Kosovo statistic institute continued its work in future years and continued working after 1999? And later on they were joined by experts from the United Nations and reinforced that way?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that UNMIK made some estimates according to the municipalities for 1998, 1999, and 2000?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have on e-court 3D422, please. It is a municipal breakdown, Your Honour, it shows municipalities in Kosovo by the OSCE Mission for Kosovo. Here it is. It is the municipal profile, Pristina, page 2, please, which shows us a table. [In English] Page 2, please. [Interpretation] Yes, may we zoom in on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But when we come to the last column, total, one-but-last column, total --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zoom down, please. Further up the document. The table above. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We're looking at the ethnic composition data for Pristina municipality from which we have the figures for 1991, 1998, and estimates for February 2000. What is your demographic explanation, Mr. Brunborg, of the almost double -- the fact that the municipality inhabitants in Pristina have more than doubled in the space of those few years?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of that question, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the relevance of that question is to establish the influence of migration on the number of the -- number of inhabitants, and I need an expert opinion to see how far migration can affect the overall assessment and figures for the municipality and inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not -- we have three elements here. We have a census, we have the number of births and deaths, and migration, the three elements we've talked about. Now we have gone on to the third element, which is migration, and I'd like to hear the witness's opinion about the possible explanations for the effect of migration on the total population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find it, I have to say, very difficult to see the relevance of events -- or figures for February 2000, which is what you're looking at, which is a period after the traumatic events that we're dealing with. But let's see where --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I can make myself clearer and perhaps the witness can help me. What I'm actually trying to say is this: Not even for 1998 was it possible to make any - how shall I put this? I'm trying to find the right word - serious prognosis, serious estimate of the number of inhabitants because the data available were extremely small, the sample was extremely small, for it to be able to provide any correct framework, or, rather, everything we obtain are in fact estimations. They cannot be considered to be exact figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we better hear if the witness can assist in any way by reference to these figures. Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two observations. First, if these numbers are correct, then there has been incredibly high migration in two years, 1998 to 2000; but secondly, it says in the footnotes to the table that the 1998 population estimate excludes forced displacement. And so it could be that the Pristina population already in 1998 included lots of people who had been forced to leave their usual residence. That's all I can say. I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And this estimate excluding forced displacement was the UNHCR assessment that you used, estimate that you used?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, the French demographer used that. The report doesn't say whether the -- to my knowledge, whether it was included or not, the forced displacement in that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the UNHCR material was for 1998, I think, and this one's for the 9th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. The OSCE estimate. I just wanted to show this to the witness and ask him if he included this information in his own report, whether he processed this material when he made his own estimations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the estimates were not made by me. I interpreted the estimates, but if the estimates are for the whole country, it doesn't matter whether displaced migration or -- is included or not because it's minus in one area and plus in another area of the country. So for the total population, it doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm -- it's not clear to me, Mr. Visnjic, but perhaps it should be. Are you contesting the estimate of the population as immediately prior to the war as estimated by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no. I'm just trying to establish whether the witness had enough data and information to provide us with what he has given us. Or I'm challenging everything, in other words, until the witness shows me that he used all this data in compiling his report and telling us what he's telling us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, we're not happy that this should continue. We think that time is not being productively used at all here at the moment. Unless there's a particular issue you want the witness to address, then we think you should bring your cross-examination to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what are they about, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are about, Your Honour, the report 2002, page 8, paragraphs 2, 3, and 4, and the estimates for the migration that the witness quotes in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let us hear what your first question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this:

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your report - and I'm referring to the last -- or, rather, the last paragraph of page 7 and the first three on page 8, you says that -- you said that migration was between 15.900 and 911000. 911.000.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 159.000; interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the first full paragraph on page 8, third -- fourth last line. Now, what's the question, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd like the witness, as an expert, to explain to me and to give me his expert opinion on the value of these estimates, since they differ six times over, compared to the estimate of 159.000, and this other estimate, where it is estimated that the number is 911.000, 911.000 people who migrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the 159.000 figure?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last paragraph, Your Honour. [In English] "The difference between this figure and the estimate for population on 1st of October, 1998, amounting to between 159.000."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, may you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the third paragraph at page 8, it says that the estimate of the migration is between -- from 1981 to 1998 is between 159.000 and 246.000. In the previous paragraph it says that is between 611 and 911.000, but that includes 1999. It's from 1981 to 1999. And as we all know, there was very heavy out migration, especially in the first half of 1999, due to the escalation of the conflict. And the uncertainty refers particularly to the number of out migrants in that period, and that's why -- that is why there's much more uncertainty about migration in 1999 than in the previous years. And also then the migration for the, let's say, 17-year period, 1981 to 1998, is much smaller than the 18-year period in 1981 to 1999. So I think this is consistent. These figures are absolutely consistent and logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that main paragraph there you talk about the UNHCR 1999 estimate. Now, is that something different from what you were talking of at the beginning of the report when you first refer to the UNHCR figures? That's on page 2 in the third-last paragraph, where you talk about an estimate for 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- I have to -- this is confusing even to me, so I need to be absolutely certain. The UNHCR has two estimates. One is for 1998, which is a projection of the 1991 population is 2.188.817 people. The second estimate is a headcount made in -- later for 1999, August 1999, which is 1.560.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- million people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So if I've understood you correctly, in this estimate of the 600 -- from 611 to 911.000, this includes 1999 as well. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And if we now subtract the period from 1981 to 1998 - and I just leave 1999 - then I will obtain the figure of about, depending on what data you use, between 450 to 550.000 people migrating in 1999. Is that right? Is that what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I didn't do the calculation, but I trust you all do that during this, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you because I'm not very strong in arithmetic. Perhaps you could help me.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that there are ranges given for all of these figures, low and high estimates, so really you have to be very careful when you subtract that you get -- you subtract in the right way, but it's probably not -- it's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now if I look at 1999 now, when you tell me the -- when you say the number of migrations, does that imply what you told me earlier on, emigration and immigration?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, you have to specify -- we have to point to the specific sentence. It's usually -- here it is usually net migration, which is out migration minus in migration, but some estimate could concern only out migration. In a war situation, we talk about refugees, which is obviously out migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All I wanted to ask you is this: If this data is correct and if we assume that this period was calculated for 1999 and if we agree that it was between 450.000 and 550.000 people, then what does this figure contain methodologically speaking? Does it include people who left Kosovo or who returned to Kosovo or quite simply can you explain what that figure represents, how did you arrive at that number, regardless of whether it's correct or not, but what does it mean? What does the number actually signify?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think there was also an -- attempts to estimate the return migration. Yes, when the survey was done by the French demographers and UNFPA, they asked whether there were members of the household who had been absent and including those who had returned. So these are net migration because they -- they asked how many had left, if anybody absent, and when they left, and if somebody returned. So both -- both numbers can be estimated, depending on the focus and the interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, on that note, we will break. We need a 20-minute break at this stage, and we hope to return to greater focus. Could you meanwhile, Mr. Brunborg, leave with the usher, who will show you where to wait during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I take my papers with -- notes with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we'll resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brunborg, the way I understood the methodology or the way used by the French demographers, which was used by them for one of their surveys, they used the sample method. Am I right in concluding that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The sample was based on the population's presence on the spot. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was a three-stage sample so they first selected areas and then later interviewed everybody in a given area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: As you explained to me just before the break, you assume that the figure corresponds to net migration. That's the way I understand it, and I apologise if I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, because, as I said, they recorded absent household members and subtracted those who were -- had returned. That's my understanding also, but both numbers can be calculated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Their survey reflects the situation at that moment, the situation in the field. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it did not envisage a situation which -- well, first of all, when was it conducted?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was conducted in November 1999 and February 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If a person left Kosovo and then returned before February 1999 -- sorry, November 1999, that person would not have been recorded as part of this survey. Am I correct in concluding that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. It would be recorded as somebody who had been away and included in the out migration streams from Kosovo and then again be included in the population count as of November 1999. Because there is a question in the survey about the usual members and whether someone has been away and whether somebody is absent at the time of the survey.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this: If a person had left Kosovo after September 1998 and returned before January 1999, since the census or the survey was done in November 1999, would that person have been included in this survey as an -- as a person who emigrated?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I need to check. First they ask whether the person was present on the 1st of October, 1998, and they ask about for each household person whether the person is present or temporarily absent. And they ask for absent persons. They ask how long did he or she stay away, number of months, number of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is still unclear to me. Can you address my specific question, please. If the person left Kosovo after September 1998 -- well, let me put it this way. After the 1st of October, 1998, and returned to Kosovo before January 1999, would that person be recorded as part of the survey as someone who emigrated?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, he would be recorded by somebody who had been absent and had returned. So he would be included in the gross migration flow from Kosovo in 1998 or 1999, depending on when the person left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He would also -- that person would also be recorded as being present on the 1st of October, 1998, which was the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So on the face of it they would not be part of a net migration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The results we discussed at the beginning, this being the figures of 600 -- excuse me. 900.000 -- I'm just trying to find the exact figure. 600.000 and 900.000, or rather, as we calculated, between 450 and 550.000 of those who emigrated in 1999 that would be net migration, if I understand it correctly?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, I think so -- well, no. It says left Kosovo so that is left -- so that is gross out of migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not sufficiently clear. The estimates of migration, say the 911.000 figure is that gross or net in terms of estimate? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm also not so clear. That must be net. The authors of the French report are -- I'm sorry, are not so clear on this, but this must be net migration, since it's the result of a difference between different population figures. So that's the net.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If that is correct, based on your overall knowledge, what would be your expert opinion as to the value or weight of these estimates if, according to the issues just discussed, there are 450 or 550.000 people who appear as being the figure pertaining to net migration from Kosovo and this survey was conducted in November 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have to say, Mr. Visnjic, that I don't understand that figure of 450 to 550.000. So perhaps you or the witness could illuminate that point for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I did do the arithmetics in the intermission and the break, and I found that the -- in 1999 the net migration was between 452.000 and 665.000 by subtracting the total migration in the 18-year period 1981 to 1999, so roughly half a million.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You've assisted me with the exact figures, 452 to 665.000. Does that tally with this possibility, that between the 1st of November, 1999, and February 2000 when your first estimate was given, does it still mean that the most part of these people, the figure between 452 and the 665.000 people were still in Kosovo but left after 1998?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's my interpretation of these figures, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know I am trying your patience, but I will try to be quick with the next exhibit and it is 3D423. It is Urosevac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, I wanted to ask you to comment a piece of information which states that as of October 1999 the population in Urosevac was 96.967. The next estimate was for the year 2000, amounting to 140 -- it is the second page. It is 143.845. Here as well we have extreme migration, it seems, for the period of only a few months. In Exhibit 3D424, in which case we are discussing Vucitrn municipality, the case appears to be the same. It also refers to the year 1999, the figure is 97.723; for the year 2000, 102.662. And then the next Defence Exhibit 3D421 concerning Podujevo municipality, the figure is 122.000 in 1999, and 131.300 in 2000. Mr. Brunborg, this is data for Pristina and surrounding -- the surrounding municipalities. Why did I focus on these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the last one you gave was 122.000, compared with, you said, 131.300. Now that's not a figure on the screen; 125.968 is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. You are correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the figure we should be paying attention to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the figure you have on the screen. However, I have the figure of 131.300, which seems plausible to me, although I am aware that there may have been a mistake. In any case, I wasn't going to focus on the exact figure but on the general increase in numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, I showed you the figures for Pristina, where the figures almost doubled. I will now focus on the adjacent municipalities, trying to confirm my thesis, which is that people moved from one area to another, from one municipality to another, or from the municipalities adjacent to Pristina into Pristina itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the witness is not in a position to deal with material of this nature that he's not had previous dealings with. He told you he had not seen this before, and if you have a proposition, a thesis, to develop about where people moved to and from, then that's a matter you can develop in your own case. The witness has already said that as far as he's concerned his interest is in the overall figures, which means that some will be lower in one -- they'll be lower in one area, higher in another, but it's the overall figure that matters for the purpose of his evidence. So let's concentrate on the issues that he's qualified to give evidence on rather than try to build up a Defence case in court on material he's never seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. [In English] Sorry, thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I merely wanted to see what the material studied by the witness was when he arrived at some conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My last question is this: Are you familiar with the work of Dr. Rifat Biljaku [phoen] who was a Kosovo demographer, and the title of his work is The Demographic Development of the Population of Kosovo. In his data for 1999 and -- 1992 and 1993, we find the figure of 370.000 Albanians abroad as early as that time. Were you familiar with his work and did you use that to make conclusions in your study?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not familiar with this work, but I've seen other references to very large numbers of Albanians being abroad for work. And so this figure here is entirely consistent with the other figures. Now, whether these people should be included with the population of Kosovo is a matter of discussion. If they are away for more than a year, they should not be included according to international standards. If they left the family for a short while then and are coming back for vacation and otherwise, then they should be included in the de jure population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: According to the best of your knowledge and your assessment, were these people included or not, irrespective of their numbers? Were they included in the estimates you addressed?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They were obviously not included in the UNFPA Blayo study -- well, if they were members of the households, then they were -- sorry, I have to think. Then they may have been included. That's right. But if there are whole households who had left, we have to distinguish between whole households and members of households. And if members of households had left, then -- and their household members back in Kosovo were interviewed, then they would probably include those who were temporarily absent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The criterion that you've just given of being absent for more than a year, was that applied by the Blayo study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They interviewed everybody, so their definition of what is a household member is really up to the respondents. They asked for how long these temporarily members had been absent, so it was up to the authors, Blayo et al., to leave out those who had been absent for more than a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know if that's what they did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this was a de facto estimate and so they were left out, those who were temporarily absent, and they did not make a de jure estimate. But they did include them in the migration streams since 1981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
