utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My last question: Did you consult the EU data on the immigration from Kosovo into the countries of the EU, before the period you were asked to provide your opinion on of course?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not directly, but the Blayo study gives a number of Albanians in various European countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Based on what you have explained here or based on the data of the EU?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Based on data of EU. I think -- let me see. No, they asked -- sorry, Blayo asked, they asked in the survey in which country their temporarily absent household members were. So that's it. They did, however, contact Switzerland to ask about Albanians in Switzerland and their age and gender and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know why Albanians migrate to Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most of them to work. Now after in 1999 there were of course many who left because of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it easier for them to migrate to Switzerland than to an EU country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shouldn't think so. Various countries have different migration policies and already accepted 6.000 refugees from Kosovo in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask the witness something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The only country that the data was compared with was Switzerland and none of the EU countries were consulted. Do we agree on that, because my question focused on the countries of the EU. And I'm trying to recall, but I believe Switzerland is still not an EU member. And if we agree on that, I'm willing to conclude my cross-examination. I'm asking about the data, not about Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I did not consider EU data, and I don't think the Blayo et al. did consider the EU data.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll have just a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Brunborg. My name is Branko Lukic. I appear on behalf of General Lukic in these proceedings, and I will have a few questions for you. Based on your report and your testimony today, may we conclude that concerning the number of the population in Kosovo there is no reliable data. There are only estimates.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I would say they are reliable estimates and showing that the general picture is one of quite rapid population growth to somewhat more than 2 million in 1998. But you are right, there are no exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we also agree that the most unreliable part is precisely the one you indicated; that is, the migration of the population?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, that is a very -- is always a very difficult piece of information in all statistical -- in all statistics for all countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: If I may, the survey by the French demographers did ask about migration. So in some way it is better than the migration data during the -- from the official statistical office in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When discussing official data from Belgrade, can we agree that their data is also based on estimates?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, except for census years, and I did not remember if there is a question relating to migration in the censuses. But otherwise, all migration figures they might present for non-census years are based on estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree as well that compared to the other two categories, after 1991 [Realtime transcript read in error "1999"] the data relayed to Belgrade were also based on estimates rather than on specific verifiable facts?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, after 1991 they continued to relay population and death figures for some years, but they did not have any migration figures, so there were no -- they did not relay any migration figures to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The estimates include the birth and death rates as well, because after 1991 there were no further censuses. Therefore, Belgrade was also estimating?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of absolute numbers on births and deaths, they estimated rates for births and deaths, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, line 20 there, should that be after 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday at page 36, line 5 of the transcript, you said that it is normal that people move en masse because of wars. Can we agree that there was a war in Kosovo in 1998 as well, before the 1st of October of that year?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I think there is a mistake in the translation. It referred to yesterday and I was not -- I was not here yesterday. So you probably meant before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Maybe I misspoke, I don't know, but in any event I meant today, yes.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't have detailed knowledge about the Kosovo conflict in 1998. I believe there was some migration then -- out migration then too. All indications are that, but the most serious conflict was in 1999. The -- based on the Blayo report, I have made some estimates on the number of migrations from -- in 1998 and it was 38.250.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, for the entire 1998 until the 1st of October of that year, according to you, there were 38.250 people who emigrated from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think that it was for all of 1998, according to my notes and my reading of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take you back just briefly to an earlier answer about deaths -- births and deaths. Was there in the 1990s no system of recording births and deaths in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was. But the previous Defence lawyer referred to the fact that there was some interruption in the recording of these births and deaths. I think it was 1997, wasn't it? Yes. But before then I believe that it was the -- these events were recorded as usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your report you also note that the Albanians boycotted the population census. Do you know that the Albanians from Albania immigrated to Kosovo and Macedonia in their masses and that that, in fact, was the reason why the Albanians boycotted the population census, because the -- a census registers just the citizens of one country. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't know the details about that and the political background on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. Mr. Lukic, I've -- I waited until the question was answered in this case, but -- just to be absolutely sure, but that's not an appropriate question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness in his report mentioned Macedonia as well and Kosovo. So that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's not the point. The point is the reason for the boycott of the census, and that's not a matter that he is qualified to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brunborg, did you in the course of your work discover how many Albanians in Kosovo who were actually citizens of the state of Albania?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I did not come across any information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that not even the federal statistics institute was ever able to establish how many Albanians from the state of Albania were living in Kosovo? Did you come across that piece of information from the institute of statistics in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, and that does not surprise me that they did not know because for knowing that they would need to have a census and ask about their citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree over the following. You were not able to provide a precise number of inhabitants and the ratio between the national groups on the 1st of January, 1999. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I was not asked to provide numbers for 1999, only for 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you because our indictment begins on the 1st of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: So I think that I have been able to provide fairly precise figures for 1st of October, 1998, that is only --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your report I was surprised by one portion where you say that you found data saying that the Serbs from Serbia proper came to inhabit Kosovo. So could you tell me the source. Where did you come across that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think in the general literature. I need to -- I need to consult my report, which was written several years ago. Malcolm writes about emigration from Kosovo. Can you enlighten me on where you found that information, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] That's a question. Give me one second. It's page 7, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Migration into Kosovo of Serbs and Croatians, Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war period 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Serbia proper I guess that is.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, the Croatians and Bosnians were refugees, many of them, or displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right. But let me try to find --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I see also you referred to settlement of Serbs from central Serbia and Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I do not recall now but I've read that in the literature. It could be Malcolm, it could also be other sources. I believe that there was -- for a while there was a programme for -- to settle Serbs in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But never implemented. That's why I'm asking you whether you found the exact data, how many Serbs from proper -- Serbia proper went to Kosovo to live there.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's right. I did not find any data, so that's why I did not mention --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: -- include them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. That were all my questions I have for you. Thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Brunborg, that completes your evidence at this trial. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give evidence. You're now free to leave us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz -- Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's next witness is Zlatomir Pesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you want to ask something in relation to this witness, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. This witness was originally noticed as a live witness. We proposed to offer his written statement and a supplemental information to that statement and also lead some live evidence from him, so he's what I referred to in the past as a combination witness, live and 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but I think I read somewhere about the likelihood of an extended examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the most recent notification we gave referring to him did mention Rule 92 ter and live and an hour and a half of live testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the latest one I've got estimates three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I based that partly on having how sat in some proofing with him earlier this week. He's a very deliberate witness who speaks slowly and carefully after a pause between questions. He'll be a delight for the translators and the court reporter when he's being questioned in his own language, I think, but it does take longer to go through things with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what does his evidence relate to principally?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is -- he was a career soldier, and he will be testifying about organisation and structure in the VJ. His job in 1999, from January 1999, he was transferred to the military district, where he was principally responsible for conscription and mobilisation of the recruits and dealt with the military districts, the military sectors, and the military detachments, which is something different from the VJ, which he can explain to you better than I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how does that tie in with your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, we have alleged that the crimes committed were by forces under the control of these accused, and during wartime you have heard and will hear evidence about how the forces -- how various forces are subordinated to the VJ, not only the MUP, but the military territorial detachments. And his evidence goes to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that he doesn't purport to give any evidence about any criminal conduct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Very little in that regard, Your Honour. He touches on it, and he's talking about the reservists from the VJ as well, how they are activated and used during times of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's now your best estimate of the live part of his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with his statement I think two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find that very surprising in view of the content of this evidence and its relevance to the case. It may be nice to have a very complete picture of the military structure, but the statement itself goes into a lot of that detail, and I just wonder what you're going to do for two and a half hours with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sure you'll be watching me closely, and if you determine that I'm wasting time you'll bring it to my attention. But I think it is relevant and it will tie in with evidence yet to be heard on the military. He will talk about some documents, and in going through his statement I discovered that in answering one question the answer often elicited several questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we're agreed that careful monitoring of the progress of the evidence may lead us to curtail the time spent, but we shall see. So let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- have the witness in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pesic. Can you hear me? Would you now make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document being placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Pesic, you'll be asked questions by a number of counsel in turn. The first counsel to examine you will be for the Prosecution, and then later counsel for the various accused. So we'll start with counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. Would you please state your name for the record and spell your last name.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Zlatomir Pesic, P-e-s-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand you're a retired VJ or JNA colonel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, prior to coming here today did you have occasion to be interviewed by and give a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal on the 29th and 30th of January, 2004?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I may ask the usher to hand him a hard copy. And, Your Honours, this is Exhibit P2502.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recognise that document as the statement you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And earlier this week, actually yesterday, did you have occasion to speak with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor after having reviewed your statement, and did you note some changes that you would like to make to that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm now handing him Exhibit 2515, P2515.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to see that document which is marked as a supplemental information?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are typing errors; however, they're not essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does that document reflect the changes that you noticed that you wanted to make to your 2004 statement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With those changes noted in that supplement, are you now satisfied and able to attest to this Court that your statement is true and accurate and that if you were asked those same questions you would give the same answers now under oath?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender the statement with the supplemental information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, your military career is set out in your statement in paragraphs 2 and 3 and partly in paragraph 4. I note that you in 1977 to 1988 were with the guards division. Can you tell us what the guards division of the JNA was.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: One of the operative units of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or rather, the Army of the Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there anything special or unique about that particular division?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Nothing special, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you say that you attended the command staff academy in 1988/1989, as that was a prerequisite for becoming a colonel. When did you, in fact, become a colonel?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I note that in 1995 to 1999 you were the assistant for logistics on the command staff of the Pristina Corps. Who was your immediate superior? Who was the head of logistics on the Pristina Corps command staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: I took over the duty in December 1995. I became assistant for logistics on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm afraid maybe I didn't make my question clear. Who was -- was there anyone else above you in terms of dealing with logistics, or does that title mean that you are the primary person responsible for logistics?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of the command of the Pristina Corps, that was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's my misunderstanding about the term. What were your duties as the assistant for logistics?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: To provide logistics and support to all the units of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 we see that you were appointed commander of the Pristina Military District in January of 1999. First of all, tell us who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The military district was subordinate to the commander of the 3rd Army, so the appointment to that duty was something that was decided by the commander of the 3rd Army, and it was pursuant to his order and decree that I was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was that person at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: At that time it was General Nebojsa Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you explain for me and the Judges, please, who -- regarding military districts, how do they relate to the VJ, to the Yugoslav army? Are they a part of the army? Something separate and distinct? Could you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Military districts are military territorial organs. Specifically speaking, the military district of Pristina covers the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps and carries out assignments for the need of the Pristina Corps and further afield as well. The basic task is to carry out their military duties and assignments. To carry out the military duties which comprise the introduction of adults or men of military age into the registrar -- register, to recruit them, to recruit young men, and send them to do their military training and military service, to take them on after they have completed their military service, and to keep records of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As I understand it in the FRY at the time, every young man when he reached the age of 18 had an obligation to perform national service in the military. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: When they reached the age of 18, they would be recorded in the military -- listed in the military records, in the military register, when they become of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And by -- was there a requirement then that they actually serve in the military at some point in time after they reached the age of 18?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Certainly, pursuant to the law governing the army when the young men reached the age of 18 - and now it is 21 - they had a duty to perform their military service with certain exceptions. And if you were exception, you could postpone this, due to sickness, to further education, or to being abroad, and some other specific reasons that can be taken onboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there any way you could avoid it entirely or merely delay it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The law regulated serving your -- doing your military service by the age of 27 and exceptionally by the age of 35. Then special procedure would be put in place for automatically becoming a member of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the minimum term you had to serve was how long?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: In the period we're discussing, it was 12 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did it apply to all ethnic groups in the former Republic of Yugoslavia or were some excluded?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: It applied to all citizens. All citizens had to do their military service, regardless of their ethnicity or religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As a practical matter, were some groups omitted or excluded from the requirement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the term "groups." What you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any particular ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: I have just said that all citizens are required to do their military service, all citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, regardless of their religion or their faith and their nationality or ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understood that answer that it was the requirement by the law. My question was: As a matter of practice, did that differ from what the law was.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: That is how the law regulated the matter. Now, if you mean specifically in Kosovo, for example, then that is a separate case, a separate matter, and I'm not in a position to give you a precise answer to that because I occupied my post and performed my duties from January 1999, and I don't know the period of time or as of what moment the members of the Albanian ethnic group from Kosovo were not called up to do their military service, or weren't included in the register and were not sent to complete their military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But that did happen in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes. But not for Albanians living in other areas of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, did the assistant for logistics have any responsibilities in relation to the mobilisation of young men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm referring to the period when I took over the duty of the person in charge of the military district who was in charge of conscripts. While I was with the logistics in the corps until January 1999, that was not part of my duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But from January 1999, that was your primary duty, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that already the situation in Kosovo when you assumed the post as head of the Pristina Military District in January 1999? That is, that Albanians from Kosovo were not being conscripted and were not on your rosters for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. What I found upon my arrival was that the documentation pertaining to the Albanian ethnic group which had served the military term and that they were made part of the reserve force; however, they were not deployed within the units of the corps or of the military district. As for the young Albanians who were of age, they were no longer made part of the registry -- of the register.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in -- in the former Yugoslavia when I reach the age of 18, I'm obligated, absent some exception, to serve my military duty for a year. When a person completes that one year of his military obligation, what happens when he leaves the army? Does he keep his uniform or his weapon or does he turn everything in? What happens?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: After one has served his military duty, his military term, the soldier returns home in civilian clothes with his military booklet, which had been stamped in his unit, stating the date of completion of the military service. His personal file is being sent by his unit to the military district by mail; to be specific, to one of the offices of the military district. Within one week, the soldier is duty-bound to report to the military district to confirm his arrival. And as of that moment, the office in -- within the military district in charge puts the person on the list of the reserve forces. Depending on the needs and applications made by units and corresponding to his military specialty, that person is then given a unit and given wartime deployment, which is registered in his file and in his military booklet. Later, he can be summoned or drafted by the unit itself through the military district or via the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. I have a question about that. When you say he can be summoned or drafted by the unit itself, do you mean the unit that he was on active duty with prior to leaving the army and becoming a part of the reserve?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: No, no. The unit that the person had been assigned to by the military district, depending on the given person's military specialty. As to what unit it can be, it doesn't have to be within the military district or the garrison itself; he can be with another unit. His wartime deployment is with the units within the territory where he lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would that depend in large part upon what his military specialty was and where a need was for someone with that specialty?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would. Upon recruitment, the recruiting office with the military district needs to pay attention to the military specialist -- the specialty, the so-called "ves," v-e-s in B/C/S, and they try to match that to the units within the given territory. The manning itself is done by the military district, in this case the Pristina Military District, taking into account the needs of the units within its area. He is not going to be sent to the navy, in other words, if there are no navy units within the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after I have been 18 and done by active service and now I'm 19 and gone home and I'm in the reserves, how long would one remain in the reserve forces? Was there a time-limit after which I would no longer have an obligation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: One's military duty begins when one turns 18 and concludes when one is 55, pursuant to the Law on Military Duty; or, to be more specific, the Law on National Defence which comprises the provisions pertaining to the military duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Now, military districts, was the entire former Republic of Yugoslavia divided into military districts or was that only in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: To use the official term, military district, the entire territory was divided into military districts, the military district of Pristina, of Nis, of Kragujevac, of Uzice, of Belgrade, of Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in Kosovo, the province of Kosovo, how many military districts were there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: There was one military district covering the units in the territory of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: And it had five military branches within its framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I know in your statement at paragraph 6 you mention that there were five military sectors, is how it's translated into English. Is that the correct term, "vojni odsek"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the sectors were further divided into military territorial detachments?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had detachments, the so-called "odseci" in B/C/S in smaller towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And geographically were those detachments found in each of -- each of the municipalities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Military sectors covered larger municipalities, those being Pristina, Kosovska Mitrovica, Prizren, and Gnjilane. In smaller municipalities and larger local communes, there were detachments of the sectors. For example, the Pristina Military Sector had a detachment in the municipality of Podujevo, then another one in the municipality of Urosevac, another one in the municipality of Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now I want to go to -- thank you for that. I want to go to paragraph 9 of your statement where you explain that the military territorial groups were responsible for dealing with compulsory service and mobilisation of the reserves. In your supplemental information to paragraph 9, you indicated that most reservists had their uniforms already. When had they obtained their uniforms? Were they issued to them when they arrived after their active-duty service or how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Once the men of military age are being assigned their respective units, that unit relays to him where the assembly points at wartime are once general mobilisation is declared or if being issued with a summons or a draft call. If the given unit has clothes, uniforms, at its disposal, the unit issues the uniform to the soldier. In case he is not given one, that is dealt later during mobilisation. Units were prepared for that. They had spare clothing, which would then be distributed to those men who had no uniforms and belonged to the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Partially, as a result of this process, is it fair to say that the reservists who were activated in March of 1999 had a variety of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your -- oh, I'm sorry, did you want to go on?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: It is true that they had different uniforms at the moment of mobilisation. That was due to several reasons. Some of them were older and they had been issued with uniforms previously and were given the -- then uniform, the then-type of uniform. Men who were younger and who were issued with uniforms at a later stage received the new type of uniform. In any case, the intention was that the old uniforms be replaced with the new ones. In some units, this had been implemented and some it had not, depending on their resources and the orders of their respective commands. There were also special units, special police and reconnaissance units, which were regularly issued with the new type of uniform. These priority units had newer uniforms, and this is how the variety of uniforms in existence at that time is explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the primary distinction between what you referred to as the old uniforms and the new-type uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The update, the general update of the army, including the introduction of new uniforms, which were different by way of quality, colour, and another distinction was that pertaining to caps and berets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if you intend going into the detail of the appearance of the uniforms, then that will be after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, we have to break now for half an hour. While we have that break, could you please leave the courtroom. The usher will show you where to wait. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I was just asking you about paragraph 9 in your supplemental information. You mentioned the difference between old and new-type uniforms. Were the old uniforms the solid colour green that sometimes was referred to as SMB I think? SMB?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in small numbers. The reserve forces who were of older age and these uniforms were no longer supplied at a certain stage because the envisaged change to the new-type uniforms for the younger recruits was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you described those as green camouflage. I wasn't clear, though, when you mentioned the military detachments and you described those as reconnaissance units. These were priority units that had newer uniforms. Was that also the green camouflage or was that something different? Were there two types of green camouflage?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The standard name was SMB. That was the oldest type of uniform, and I believe our reserve forces nowadays no longer have it. Later on there was a green uniform, similar to the SMB, but it was a different fit and colour. And then the M-77 and the M-80, M-90, and M-91 appeared. I believe it was a standard procedure of introducing new uniforms; however, it couldn't be done overnight in any army, including ours. Usually priorities are given to the units, the so-called A units, and then the B units, and then in order of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The M-77, M-80, M-90, and M-91, were those all green camouflage of some sort?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: For the most part. The prevailing colour, however, is this green-grey camouflage colour corresponding to our terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does SMB stand for anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is "sivo maslinasto boja" in B/C/S, olive-grey.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, olive-green.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hesitated to ask the question in a leading way. I'm glad now I didn't. We've heard a number of witnesses refer to uniforms as olive-grey-green. Is that something other than SMB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I believe it to be the same thing. There may be nuances with the new camouflage patterns to resemble the uniforms of some western armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- in an earlier answer you just mentioned the so-called A units and the B units. In paragraph 10 of your statement, you talked about two classifications of military territorial detachments A and B. Is that what you were referring to up above?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: No. These are detachments in the sense of a unit formation, the level. It's a different thing. As for A-type formations with the army, I mean their manning strength and the percentage is higher at peacetime; therefore, at wartime they needed less men, as opposed to the B units, which had less personnel and they drew more from the reserve forces. They were less mobile.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were those smaller B units located in the smaller municipalities or was there any correlation between the unit size and the municipality where they were from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The explanation I gave as for the A and B formations, it is a general principle used in the army. Perhaps to explain it better I could say that the modernisation process in terms of introducing new types of uniform did not have much to do with the A and B classification of the detachments with fell under my military district. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, under my military sectors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I should continue explaining. The A detachments, only A formations could be manned from a given territory. As for the B formations, the municipalities they were in simply had not enough -- did not have enough population. This is the only distinction: They could not be fully manned from their respective municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could men be pulled in then from other municipalities to fill up those detachments or was that not permitted?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: These are detachments of the military district, or military sectors, and I said that a military sector comprises a set territory with a number of municipalities, one larger municipality and several smaller ones, and I quoted the example of Pristina. And more specifically, in Pristina you could form an A-class detachment with 400 men. Urosevac, for example, did not have enough men, enough people, and so it had a detachment with just 200 soldiers. So that's the difference. The possibility that you have in a given location to provide a full complement of men. So this corresponded to the territory and the needs of the detachments. You would have to bring in people from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in your answer that -- before that one that it was difficult sometimes to meet the quota and fill up these detachments. In paragraph 10, you said some of these were never full strength because of a lack of non-Albanians. That was a problem for you in Kosovo, wasn't it, because there weren't that many non-Albanians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say in the last sentence in paragraph 10 that: "We did not include Albanians in these detachments." Why not? I think you told us before that that was a pre-existing condition when you took this job in January 1999. But do you know why Albanians in Kosovo were not being taken in? Was there a law or an order or a regulation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Possibly there was an order which I did not see. Possibly it was an -- for security reasons a tacit agreement; possibly it was an assessment on the part of the security organs that there should not be any Albanians within the composition of a detachment. So I'm not quite sure what the reason was, as I was in the military district as of January, and I wasn't able to look at all the previous orders and instructions and guidelines that might have been issued in that regard. So that is the state of affairs that I came upon when I joined up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. In connection with that you say in paragraph 11 in your supplemental information that the normal cut-off age for service would be 55 years of age, but later when you had a shortage of reservists this age limit wasn't strictly followed. So actually to fill up these units, were you sometimes taking men older than 55?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the units of the corps, we selected younger men and we'd fill up our detachments with the remaining men. And it is possible that there were people who were older, which wasn't anything unusual nor did anybody complain if they were called up because they were locals, they knew each other, they were units which were responsible for the territory they were in, mostly they were resident there, had assignments in the territory, so there was not -- there was -- there were no complaints or nothing to say that they could not be called up, no provisions of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because of the shortage of military-aged non-Albanian men in Kosovo, did you also have to sometimes lower your standards with regard to some of the other requirements, in terms of physical fitness or mental fitness or even criminal history?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: When it came to the detachments, let me repeat once again, they were people from the area, from that territory. They knew each other and they wanted to be in a detachment and be armed. They didn't want to be left out. They didn't want to be the exception; only if they were ill, perhaps. So there we didn't have a problem. They were territorial detachments responsible for the territory, for their families, for their neighbour's families, for their territory, so that wasn't a problem as far as these detachments were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a question. You said earlier that the -- in peacetime the military district was subordinate to the 3rd Army. During the state of war, to whom or what was the military district subordinate?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: In peacetime, the military district was subordinated to the commander of the 3rd Army. In the newly arisen situation, the army commander would decide to resubordinate the command of the military district to the Pristina Corps command for understandable reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In there where you say "the newly arisen situation," do you mean the state of war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes, the concrete situation as of March, and this happened in April -- well, there are documents about that for April. I don't have it, but they do exist. And this was regulated exclusively on the basis and pursuant to orders, strictly defined in a date with respect to the resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During peacetime you, as head of the Pristina Military District, what was your authority over the military sectors and military territorial detachments?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: I could issue orders with relation to the military sectors; they were all subordinate to me. As for the detachments, they were within the military sectors and they were subordinated to the commander of the military sector. He was responsible for having them up to full strength and for their training, et cetera, materiel, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did that change during the state of war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: At a certain point in time, yes, it did. And during a certain period practically all the detachments were subordinate to the brigade commanders in the area of responsibility of those brigades in order to avoid dual command. Dual command within the same zone or area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about the military territorial detachments in peacetime. Did they exist and function -- I mean, were men wearing uniforms and carrying out some kind of duty as part of the military territorial detachment in peacetime, or was that something that only existed on paper to be activated if and when there was a necessity, such as a war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: They existed in wartime. In peacetime, they underwent preparation; their equipment and materiel and training. They would be called up for a day or two. There was planned training in the course of a year or a two-year period, depending on the resources available for people to be called up and trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So after you took up your duties in January 1999, sometime before the NATO bombing started, 24 March, did you get ordered or requested to provide some men for the VJ, for the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: That is a normal process and the normal obligation of a military district. It is based on plans and programmes for ensuring the full strength of the Pristina Corps, which is realised pursuant to a request made from the Pristina Corps and their requirements for various specialties for different areas or deployment in brigades. And this process is a very normal process and takes place normally in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The corps units call-up the reserve force via the organs of the military sector for purposes of training, for purposes of putting on uniforms, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm trying to distinguish between the two things I understand that you did. One was that you -- you provided conscripts, those who were doing their military service for the first time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: They were, yes, conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The ones who had never done any military service before, these you helped provide as required by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: No, no. Those who had completed their military service, who had completed their military service and become trained for a certain specialty at the request of the unit of the corps, then they would be deployed there. We would hand them over to them. We would supply them with that kind of profile.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Who was responsible then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that answer doesn't tie in with what I understood you to say earlier, where -- when you were asked about the general responsibilities of the military district, you described the military district as a military territorial organ carrying out assignments for the needs of the Pristina Corps. For example, recruitment, sending recruits to do military service, taking them on after military service, and then enrolling them as reservists. So it would appear from that, that you were responsible for the initial recruitment of those who were being mobilised as young men. Have I misunderstood that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a little misunderstanding, but it is very simple. Young people, when they reach the age of 18, or rather, 19 - and today that age is 21 - are sent to do their military service. Once they return, we list them and register them as the reserve formation, the reservists. And at the request of units from its peacetime formation to wartime formations, they send in a request and we provide them to these units because our units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand certainly that part of your responsibilities. But I must have misunderstood you on the earlier part of your answer at the beginning because you described one of your assignments or one of your responsibilities as recruitment, including -- and that was -- you then went on to describe sending people to do their military service, and that suggested to me that you arranged that the young recruits would be sent for military service. And now you're indicating that your responsibilities are confined to dealing with them after they've completed their military service and become reservists. So I'm a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For as long as they have to do their military -- or, rather, they are recruits, they are -- that is from the age of 19 or 21 to 55, they are registered as such. So they're registered as being of age. They are recruited. Their specialty is determined. And their fitness is assessed, to see how fit somebody is for a given military specialty. Then they are sent to do their military service. They could be sent from Pristina to Belgrade, for instance, or Nis, or any other town throughout the country. Once they have completed their military service, he is registered as a member of the reserve force. We have these lists of people, and at the request of a unit we offer them, if I can put it that way, on the basis of the specialties they have and how these correspond to the requirements of a particular unit. So they are sent to the unit and they are on the wartime deployment of that unit; and they are called up when the mobilisation is called or they are called up to be issued uniforms or to undergo training or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis, perhaps you can clarify it, but I remain confused at the moment about whether there's any responsibility on the part of the military district for arranging the allocation of the initial recruits at 19 or, as it now is, 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you and I are in the same boat, Your Honour. I'll try and ask a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I had the same understanding as the Judge. Did the military district or the military sectors have any responsibilities in terms of conscription, the brand new recruits who've never been in the military; or was that handled by some other agency? Who signed those people up when they turned 18 or 19 or 21 and who told them it was time to go to a particular place and take a particular military specialty? Who was responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: An organ of the military sector. At age 18, they are just registered, their names are registered. Now, when they have to do their military service, the same body calls them up and sends them off to do their military service. Once they have completed military service, they take them on and register them in their register of reservists. And when units need to be brought up to strength in times of war, then the unit sends in a request and the military sector provides men for purposes of the unit and hands over their personal files and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the military sectors -- there were five military sectors under you as the military district. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes, and each sector does this for its own territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And related to that, who tells each military sector how many recruits we need from your sector for this month? Who sets those quotas?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: It's not done by month, on the basis of months; it is done on the basis of the needs of a unit, a brigade of the Pristina Corps, for example, from Prizren. The 549th Brigade, for example, needs ten reconnaissance men and it contacts the military sector in Prizren with that request. Then the military sector in Prizren offers or supplies him with the personal files of ten scouts or reconnaissance workers, which means that the unit will receive ten scouts or ten reconnaissance men. The brigade in Kosovska Mitrovica, for example, similarly needs men from peacetime to wartime and sends in a request to the military sector Kosovska Mitrovica. Kosovska Mitrovica, or the military sector of Kosovska Mitrovica then supplies those men, the men it needs, the specialists it needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you speak of the registration of in those days the 18-year-olds, were these names registered with the military district or were they registered somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is based on cooperation with the basic service, where newborn babies are registered, for example, and the military sector receives the names of people who have turned 18 and then those names are listed and their personal files compiled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We now have the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, when I've done my military service and I've come back home and I've registered as a reservist, what if -- what does someone do or what can someone do if I decide, Boy, I hate the army, I just don't like that army lifestyle, but my buddy over there is a policeman and he's got a pretty snazzy uniform and I like the way he looks and what he does. I'd like to be a policeman instead of a reservist in the army. Can he switch or is he stuck being in the army reserve for the rest of his life?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: In cooperation with the MUP, we also supply quotas for them, as we do for the army, for the army units. Now, the peacetime service for MUP is different. I don't know that we're talking about that now, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't -- I didn't know you were going to talk about the MUP, but let's talk about -- first of all, in the peacetime -- in peacetime, the military territorial district, or the military district didn't have any responsibility for providing police reserves, did they?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Well, the reserve police in peacetime does not exist. Now, for the requirements of wartime units, we supply men, we supply the reserve -- we supply the police units with the reservists at a request from the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who decided whether a recruit would go into the police reserve or into the army reserve, VJ reserve, during a time of war? How was that determination made? Did it depend on the specialty that was required?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: This was settled in peacetime because on the basis of plans and documents, units would receive their quota of men on the basis of these plans; and once a unit came up to full strength, it was up to the unit's commander after that. So it is on the basis of his plan and requirements that he calls these men up through the military sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Colonel, I'm still a little confused about how that worked with the MUP. During peacetime could certain reservists be designated that in the event of a state of emergency or imminent threat of war or war that they would go into the police when they were activated? Was that planned ahead of time or did that only occur once there was actually some extraordinary state in effect, if you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Yes. In peacetime, too, as -- just like the military units, also at the request of the MUP, they would be assigned a reserve force or reservists, usually in cooperation with the men themselves, men of that specialty. So this is the kind of cooperation that takes place in peacetime in order to select the best cadres, the best men, with the required specialties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In paragraph 11, you mentioned that when the state of war was declared in March, the reserves filled up the Pristina Corps. And then you talked about how you had tried to convince some shiptars, Kosovo Albanians, to join. How did that come about? Because you told us before that Kosovar Albanians were not included in the reserves. But once the state of war occurred, were you looking so hard for men that you tried to persuade some of the loyal Kosovo Albanians to join the army as well?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: It was not my idea; it was the decision of my superior command. Whether it was the command of the corps or of the 3rd Army or of the General Staff, I don't know, but it was their view that an Albanian unit should be formed. I received an order from my superior command stating that, and a sufficient number of uniforms was provided as well as weapons. It was our task to try and motivate some Albanian citizens. We tried to target that part of the population which was loyal and the people who thought that what the shiptar terrorists were doing was not a good thing because they inflicted evil on the Albanian population as well. This was an attempt to use -- or to join our forces so that such people could remain there to continue working and to keep their families safe. It was an attempt to jointly oppose these extremist shiptar forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I gather from your statement that you weren't successful in being able to do that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Through my offices and my information assistants as well as the chief of security and the chief of intelligence, who were familiar with the terrain, with the territory, I tried to take part; however, we were unsuccessful. I personally went to one of the larger villages in the Kosovo Polje municipality, the village of Dobrovo. The population there is 90 per cent Albanian. They all work and they are employed by the companies there. There was a large farm there, a dairy factory, a slaughter-house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Colonel, let me stop you there. I think you have answered my question that you weren't successful in persuading them. Let me move to paragraph 15 of your statement where you tell us that in the first 20 days of the war certain detachments were subordinated to the brigades, and in your supplemental information you explain that the military territorial detachments were used for three kinds of task: Number 1, protection of vital facilities; number 2, control of the territory; and number 3, combat operations against the KLA. Can you explain for us what control of the territory involved. What did a military detachment do to control the territory?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The detachments were founded on the territorial principle. They covered their respective areas with the aim of protecting the population and property. Hence, the idea that such units should control their own ground and not to be sent away to another territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just the transcript, it's 82, 22 and 23. The witness said: They covered their respective areas with the aim of protecting all of the population and whole of the property. I mean, if this can be clarified with the witness. I'm sure he said all of the population and whole of the property. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, is that the answer you gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. The entire territory, all of the population, and all property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your supplemental information on that paragraph you also say that once these detachments were activated and subordinated to brigades of the Pristina Corps, sometimes they were used for protection of units and equipment by the brigades. Once they were re-assigned or resubordinated, discipline and their assignments were made within the command of the brigade. You mentioned that the detachments consisted of local people, whereas the brigades had regular soldiers and reservists. What's the difference between a reservist in a brigade and somebody in a detachment who was resubordinated to a brigade? Could they both be people from the same town, one just happened to be a part of the detachment and the other was activated as a reservist to go to the brigade? Is there any other distinction?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: If I understand your question, you would like to know whether there was a difference between the reservist forces of the detachment, which were made part of brigades, and the reserve forces that were already under the brigade framework?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The brigades of the Pristina Corps were brought up to strength ex-territorially as well, meaning introducing men from elsewhere, usually from the military district of Nis because they had insufficient numbers of able-bodied men to man the units of the Pristina Corps. It is my conclusion that you would like to know the difference between the reservists of that origin and the reserve forces in detachments from Kosovo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, is there any other difference than that geographical difference?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the reservists in detachments and those in brigades, there is a difference. I've explained already, I believe. It was the difference in age, equipment, and training, as opposed to the reservists and brigades which -- the people who were better trained, better equipped, and who were younger and they were specialists according to the tasks of their respective brigade. They were younger than the other type of reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I'm clear, then, those in the detachments were older, less well trained, and less well equipped? Have I got that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: Certainly. The type of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In paragraph 16 you talked about some of the commanders used the detachments that were subordinated -- resubordinated to them; they used them for protection of their combat formations. Can you give us an example of that? What brigade commander used one of these detachments to protect their combat formation? And how did -- how did that work?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: When touring the detachments, I came across instances of what we are discussing here, that detachments were engaged contrary to their original purpose and then they hadn't been trained for such specific tasks, and in certain cases they were taken outside of their territory which caused discontent. As an example, I can mention the use of the units of detachments in securing the units of the 15th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what kind of unit was the 15th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The 15th Brigade is an armoured brigade predominantly equipped with tanks and APCs. The particular detachment was engaged in securing the materiel and weaponry. This violated the formation structure. In that case, that detachment lost its subordination, it fell out of the chain, and I had to go there on several occasions so as to improve the situation, to improve the way they were organised, and to seek an appointment of an active officer to command the detachment. Up until that moment, a reservist was commanding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you complain to anybody in the 15th Brigade about this?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: In my contact with the brigade commander and the commander of the battalion, whose units were secured by the men from the detachment, as well as in my discussions with the chief of the armoured units within the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the chief of the armoured units within the Pristina Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The chief was Colonel Nikolic. I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he was using a military territorial detachment consisting of older men, less well trained, and with poorer quality equipment to protect his 15th Armoured Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The reason was that they were familiar with the terrain. Some even spoke Albanian, and that was stated as the reason for employing them in such a manner so that they could carry out such specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said that you felt that these detachments were being endangered by the decision to assign them to tasks for which they had not been trained. Did you discuss this with anyone else at the Pristina Corps or at the 3rd Army level?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: No. At that time I had already been subordinated to the commander of the corps, and I tried to resolve this on the spot in direct discussions. I toured daily. I would go and see two to three detachments per day and try to deal with the situation right there and then. I spoke with the commander of the 37th Brigade and with the Chief of Staff of the 549th Brigade. There were cases in which irrespective of all -- of everything said, some detachments carried out their respective tasks in full and they were even praised for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to paragraph 18. You say that although the units of the military district were no longer subordinated to you, you did remain an information addressee for their reports regarding the situation in the field. How often were those reports generated and received by you? Was that on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC
utterances.text: The commanders of military sectors subordinated to brigade commanders were not duty-bound to forward reports to me, but they were fair and they would send a copy to me, usually by courier, if possible the same day; if not, they would do that within the next two to three days and they would send two to three daily reports. This particularly applied to Prizren and Pec because of the security situation there and the use of couriers. They would either do that or it would be done via personal contact because some of my people would go to detachments regularly, some assistants, General Dzaklic, Colonel Cvetkovic, the chief of security, Vujisic, and then they would bring back reports which could not have been sent by courier. And when I would receive such reports, two, three, or four of them at the time, I was able to sort of put together a picture of the situation in which the entire detachment was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, is this a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Well, Mr. Pesic, that completes our court sitting for today. We have to adjourn now until tomorrow. You have to return here to continue your evidence at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. Meanwhile, it is very important that you do not have any discussion with anyone at all about your evidence, either the evidence you have already given or the evidence you may yet give tomorrow. Talk about whatever you like with whomsoever you like, except the evidence. So that's it for today. Please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you again tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
